claims.summary: For any list of 32-bit values whose little-endian bytes fit at the given pointer within the 64 KiB bound, calling the array-sum export after writing those bytes always returns their wrapping 32-bit sum.
claims.statement:
∀ (p : BitVec 32) (xs : List (BitVec 32)),
  p.toNat + 4 * xs.length ≤ 65536 →
    FVA.Wasm.Exec.ReturnsAfterWrite Examples.Mem.Lifted.module p.toNat (FVA.Wasm.Exec.le32s xs) "array_sum"
      [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 p, FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 (BitVec.ofNat 32 xs.length)] [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 xs.sum]
claims.reason: The bound requires four bytes per element to fit within 64 KiB, so the list has at most 16,384 words; the statement then guarantees the wrapped sum after writing them at the pointer.
claims.name: Examples.Mem.arraySum
claims.intent:
`array_sum(p, n)`: the sum, wrapped to 32 bits, of the `n` unsigned 32-bit words `xs` that
the caller wrote at address `p`, for every array inside the module's 64 KiB memory (so
`n ≤ 16384`: the length argument never wraps).
details: Covers every 32-bit pointer and every finite list of 32-bit elements, provided the pointer plus four bytes per element is at most the initial memory limit.
The elements are written as little-endian 32-bit words. The pointer and list length are passed as i32 values; the length is reduced modulo 2 to the 32nd power if it exceeds the i32 range.
The returned i32 is the list sum using 32-bit bit-vector arithmetic, so additions wrap modulo 2 to the 32nd power.
ReturnsAfterWrite requires a fresh instance with room for the bytes under every host behavior; the call then must terminate without trapping or throwing and return exactly the specified value.
caveats: The written source uses a hexadecimal literal, but elaboration turns it into the 32-bit value 85; the elaborated statement is authoritative.
The write-fit bound also ensures the element bytes fit, but the claim does not separately state that the pointer is suitably aligned.
Only the returned value is specified; the claim does not state that the function leaves memory unchanged.

claims.summary: For every pair of 32-bit inputs, classify returns a result determined by the unsigned first input: one of five specified wrapping arithmetic or bitwise cases, and zero otherwise.
claims.statement:
∀ (x y : BitVec 32),
  FVA.Wasm.Exec.Returns Examples.Mem.Lifted.module "classify" [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 x, FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 y]
    [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32
        (match x.toNat with
        | 0 => y + 7
        | 1 => y <<< 3
        | 2 => y ^^^ 85#32
        | 3 => y * 100
        | 4 => y - 9
        | x => 0)]
claims.reason: The statement covers every pair of 32-bit inputs and specifies the intended five cases and zero otherwise, with 32-bit wrapping arithmetic.
claims.name: Examples.Mem.classify
claims.intent:
`classify(x, y)` on unsigned 32-bit ints, by the case `x`: `y + 7`, `y << 3`, `y xor 0x55`,
`100 y`, `y − 9` for `x` = 0 … 4 (wrapped to 32 bits), else 0.
details: The first input is matched as an unsigned value. The second is manipulated as a 32-bit bit vector: addition, multiplication, and subtraction wrap modulo 2 to the 32nd power; left shift is a 32-bit shift; XOR uses the fixed 32-bit mask.
Returns requires the module to be instantiable under every host behavior and every call to terminate without trapping or throwing and return exactly the specified i32.
caveats: The result is selected using the unsigned natural-number interpretation of the first argument, not its signed interpretation.
Only the first five unsigned input values have special cases; all other bit patterns return zero.
The claim specifies only the return value, not memory effects.

claims.summary: For every 32-bit input, call_scale returns the wrapping 32-bit result of applying the specified affine expression to the input and its wrapped successor.
claims.reason: For every 32-bit input, the specified bit-vector expression is the intended affine calculation on the input and its wrapped successor, with arithmetic wrapping to 32 bits.
claims.name: Examples.Mem.callScale
claims.intent: `call_scale(x)` on unsigned 32-bit ints: `(3x + 1) + (3(x + 1) + 1)`, wrapped to 32 bits.
details: The input and all intermediate arithmetic are 32-bit bit vectors. Multiplication by three, additions, and the increment of the input all wrap modulo 2 to the 32nd power.
Returns requires instantiability under every host behavior and that every call terminates without trapping or throwing and returns exactly the computed i32.
caveats: The formula is expressed entirely in 32-bit bit-vector arithmetic, so intermediate additions and multiplications wrap; it is not an unbounded-integer arithmetic formula.
The claim says nothing about memory effects.
